source.title: Do Transformers Need Three Projections? Systematic Study of QKV Variants
source.authors: Ali Kayyam; Anusha Madan Gopal; M. Lewis

record.tranche_reason: The study compares validation perplexity with downstream benchmark performance across attention variants and explicitly argues that perplexity does not reliably predict downstream rank. It does not test the proposed scaling laws themselves.
record.gate_note: The paper reports language-model perplexities and downstream scores for different attention variants, but does not sweep parameters, tokens, or compute to fit or test power laws. Its downstream comparison bears on V6; the other reported architecture and efficiency results do not establish the scaling-law versions.
record.test_reason: The study compares attention-projection variants (QKV, K=V, GQA, MQA and combinations) at two fixed sizes (300M, 1.2B) on about 10B tokens. It cites Kaplan and Hoffmann only in passing. It runs no sweep over parameters, tokens or compute, and fits no power law. Its one result near a version is that small validation-perplexity gaps across architecture variants at a single 1.2B scale don't track the 5-shot downstream averages. V6 is about downstream performance improving predictably with scale or with pretraining loss. This comparison doesn't measure that: perplexity gaps are within about 4%, no uncertainty is reported, and most benchmark scores sit near chance (HellaSwag about 25-26%, ARC-C about 19-23%, WinoGrande about 48-51%). The measure therefore can't show whether downstream accuracy follows loss. The finding is recorded under fits_no_version, not as a test of V6. Parameter counts also differ across variants (1,033M to 1,215M) and only the attention mechanism changes, not depth or width, so V4 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right. The authors' main conclusion is that K=V projection sharing halves the KV cache with small perplexity cost (3.1% at 300M, 2.48% at 1.2B). It stacks with GQA/MQA, and relative rankings stay stable from 300M to 1.2B. On downstream tasks they say the perplexity gap doesn't translate into a comparable downstream gap. They also say perplexity is not a reliable predictor of downstream rank among variants, consistent with minor perplexity differences rarely mattering. They do not claim K=V is universally optimal.
record.recipe_differences: Compares attention projection variants and evaluates their pretraining perplexity and downstream benchmarks; it does not fit or extrapolate scaling laws or optimize parameter/token allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The downstream comparison is across attention variants and five benchmarks; the reported scores and rank relationships differ by variant and benchmark.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 1.2B attention variants, perplexity gaps of 0.5-4% don't order the 5-shot downstream averages. Q-GQA-8 has higher perplexity (5.158) than QKV (5.004) but a higher average (36.72 vs 36.40). Scores are near chance on most benchmarks and no uncertainty is given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At fixed scale, small architecture-induced differences in pretraining perplexity don't reliably predict downstream rank.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: Downstream comparisons are reported for 1.2B models only; uncertainty estimates are not reported for the benchmark scores or perplexities. The authors call some scores statistically indistinguishable but provide no corresponding uncertainty values in the supplied tables.

untested.parts: No sweep or power-law fit over parameters, tokens or compute; only two sizes at one token budget.
Attention-mechanism variants at unequal parameter counts; no depth or width variation at fixed parameters.
Vision and synthetic experiments compare architectures, not scaling form.
No downstream measurement across scale. The cross-variant perplexity versus downstream comparison is at one scale, with near-chance scores and no uncertainty.
No exponents or fitting choices compared.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'challenges' label is dropped: the comparison is cross-architecture at a single scale, with near-chance benchmarks and no uncertainty, so it doesn't test predictability with scale or loss. All six HellaSwag rows copied the Avg column instead of the HW column; the correct values are 26.15, 26.14, 26.44, 26.23, 26.13 and 25.04.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit or sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or extrapolation to larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split.
Projection-sharing variants are compared, but parameter count is not held fixed, and the study does not test depth or width effects at fixed parameter count.
No test of scaling-law form across modalities or training regimes.
Tests the relation between validation perplexity and downstream scores across 1.2B attention variants; does not test downstream predictability across model scale.
No comparison of scaling-law exponents, fitting choices, or power-law curve bending.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: 1.2B variants compared by held-out SlimPajama perplexity and 5-shot downstream benchmark scores
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that perplexity does not reliably predict downstream rank: Q-GQA-8 has a worse perplexity than QKV but a higher downstream average, while the variants' downstream averages do not follow a stable ordering by perplexity (p_qkv, p_gqa8, p_mqa, p_qgqa8, p_qmqa, d_qkv_avg, d_gqa8_avg, d_mqa_avg, d_qgqa8_avg, d_qmqa_avg).
